deck.title: The Chemical Properties of the Halogen Elements & the Hydrogen Halides

front_blocks.md: Why does the oxidising power of halogens decrease going down Group 17?

back_blocks.md: Going down Group 17, the **atomic radius** increases, so the outer shells are further from the nucleus. An incoming electron experiences greater **shielding** from the nuclear charge. The halogen's ability to attract (accept) electrons — its **oxidising power** — therefore decreases.

front_blocks.md: Bromine can displace chloride ions from a solution of NaCl.

back_blocks.md: **Chlorine** is more reactive than bromine, not the other way around. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one. Bromine cannot displace chloride ions because Cl<sub>2</sub> is the stronger **oxidising agent**.

back_blocks.md: A **hydrogen halide** is a compound formed by the reaction of a halogen with hydrogen gas (e.g. HF, HCl, HBr, HI). They are all polar covalent molecules that dissolve in water to form acidic solutions.

cards.back_md: A **hydrogen halide** is a compound formed by the reaction of a halogen with hydrogen gas (e.g. HF, HCl, HBr, HI). They are all polar covalent molecules that dissolve in water to form acidic solutions.

front_blocks.md: Describe the conditions under which H<sub>2</sub> reacts with each of F<sub>2</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.

back_blocks.md: H<sub>2</sub> + F<sub>2</sub>: **explosive**, even in cool/dark conditions. H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub>: explosive **in sunlight**. H<sub>2</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub>: reacts **slowly on heating**. H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub>: forms an **equilibrium mixture** on heating (reversible reaction).

front_blocks.md: HF is more thermally stable than HI.

back_blocks.md: **HF** has a short, strong H–F bond (fluorine is small), giving it high **thermal stability**. **HI** has a longer, weaker H–I bond due to iodine's larger atomic radius, so it is far less thermally stable.

front_blocks.md: The thermal stability of hydrogen halides **..........**  going down Group 17 because the H–X bond becomes **..........**  as the halogen atom gets larger.

back_blocks.md: The thermal stability of hydrogen halides **decreases** going down Group 17 because the H–X bond becomes **weaker** as the halogen atom gets larger.

front_blocks.md: Write the ionic equation for the displacement of bromide ions by chlorine.

back_blocks.md: Chlorine is the **oxidising agent** (it gains electrons); bromide ions are **oxidised** to bromine.

cards.front_md: Write the ionic equation for the displacement of bromide ions by chlorine.
cards.back_md:
Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) → 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) + Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)

Chlorine is the **oxidising agent** (it gains electrons); bromide ions are **oxidised** to bromine.

front_blocks.md: Explain why the thermal stability of HI is lower than that of HCl.

back_blocks.md: Iodine has a much larger atomic radius than chlorine. The **H–I bond** is longer and therefore **weaker** than the H–Cl bond. Less energy is needed to break H–I, so HI decomposes more easily on heating and has **lower thermal stability**.
